parsed_answer.content: At 3.8 years of experience, the most impactful technical implementation involves transitioning a legacy blocking I/O (BIO) file-processing service to a non-blocking I/O (NIO) architecture using Java's Selector and Channel abstractions. The legacy system relied on one thread per connection, leading to thread starvation and excessive context switching under high concurrency. By implementing a Reactor pattern with Java NIO, I decoupled the I/O multiplexing from the business logic processing. This required a deep dive into ByteBuffer management to avoid memory fragmentation and the implementation of a custom DirectBuffer pool to minimize GC pressure. The success was measured by a 60% reduction in average latency and a 4x increase in throughput capacity under load, validated through Gatling stress tests that monitored JVM heap utilization and thread state transitions.

items: NIO Selectors operate by registering Channels with an interest set (OP_READ, OP_WRITE), allowing a single thread to monitor multiple I/O events, effectively reducing the kernel-space to user-space context switching overhead.

DirectBuffers are allocated outside the JVM heap, allowing the OS to perform I/O operations directly on the memory, bypassing the need for an intermediate copy to the JVM heap, which is critical for high-performance I/O.

Exception handling in NIO requires meticulous management of the SelectionKey state; if an IOException occurs during a read/write, the key must be explicitly canceled to prevent the Selector from repeatedly returning the same faulty channel.
Success measurement requires monitoring the 'Selector.select()' blocking time and the 'pending tasks' queue size to ensure the event loop is not being blocked by long-running business logic.

parsed_answer.content: A common 'gotcha' for engineers at this level is the 'Selector wakeup' bug or the 'spurious wakeup' phenomenon. Always ensure your business logic is offloaded to a separate ExecutorService thread pool. If you perform heavy computation inside the Selector loop, you will effectively turn your NIO service back into a blocking one, negating all performance gains and causing the event loop to lag.
